A1-A2.headline: The Great Gatsby: A Famous American Story

pages.text: Have you ever wondered about the American Dream? The Great Gatsby is a famous 1925 novel by F. Scott Fitzgerald. It is set in the Jazz Age on Long Island.

pages.text: The main character who tells the story is named Nick Carraway. Nick is a young man who moves to a place called Long Island near New York City. He rents a small house next to a huge and expensive estate.

The owner of the large estate next door is Jay Gatsby. Gatsby is a very rich and mysterious man who throws huge parties. However, Gatsby is only truly interested in one thing. He wants to reunite with his former lover named Daisy Buchanan.

When the book came out in April 1925, it was a commercial disappointment. It sold fewer than 20,000 copies by October. Many people did not buy it at first, and Fitzgerald felt very sad about the sales.
Today, this book is read all over the world. Many students read it in school. It remains one of the most famous stories in American literature and history.

B1-B2.headline: The Real Life Inspirations Behind F. Scott Fitzgerald's Masterpiece

pages.text: What inspired F. Scott Fitzgerald to write his most famous book? Published in 1925, The Great Gatsby is a tragedy set during the American Jazz Age. It captures the energy and social changes of 1920s Long Island.

pages.text: The narrative draws heavily from Fitzgerald's own early life experiences. As a young man, he fell deeply in love with a wealthy socialite named Ginevra King. Her affluent family ultimately discouraged the courtship, asserting that poor young men lacked the financial standing to marry rich women.

In the novel, narrator Nick Carraway relocates to West Egg, New York, where he resides next to Jay Gatsby. An enigmatic millionaire, Gatsby hosts lavish parties while harboring a singular obsession: to rekindle his past romance with Daisy Buchanan.

Despite glowing praise from literary contemporaries like T. S. Eliot, the novel proved to be a commercial disappointment upon its initial release. It sold fewer than twenty thousand copies during its first year, leaving Fitzgerald disheartened and anxious about his career.

Fitzgerald's personal struggles and romantic disappointments directly shaped the tragic trajectory of his characters. Today, the novel is celebrated worldwide for its poignant critique of wealth, class, and social ambition.

C1-C2.headline: Disillusionment and the American Dream in The Great Gatsby

pages.text: Through the retrospective lens of narrator Nick Carraway, F. Scott Fitzgerald's 1925 masterpiece, The Great Gatsby, interrogates the moral permissiveness and hedonistic undercurrents of the 1920s.

pages.text: The genesis of the novel is deeply rooted in Fitzgerald's formative disappointments, most notably his thwarted romance with socialite Ginevra King. The socioeconomic stratification of the era—encapsulated by the rigid barrier between inherited wealth and marginalized ambition—informed Gatsby's relentless pursuit of Daisy Buchanan.

Upon publication, the work suffered a lukewarm commercial reception, generating disappointing sales figures that left Fitzgerald feeling alienated and convinced of his eventual obscurity. He died in 1940 believing his literary contributions had been entirely forgotten by the public.

A dramatic resurgence occurred during World War II when the Council on Books in Wartime distributed thousands of complimentary volumes to overseas military personnel. This unexpected dissemination catalyzed a profound scholarly re-evaluation of the text.

Subsequent academic discourse has consistently positioned the novel as a quintessential critique of the American Dream. Scholars analyze how Fitzgerald's narrative exposes the corrosive erosion of foundational ideals within a relentlessly materialistic society.
